Marital is an adjective that means relating to marriage — specifically, anything that belongs to, comes from, or is connected with the state of being married or the relationship between spouses.

Think of it this way: marriage creates a bond, a legal status, and a shared life between two people. Everything that flows from that — the happiness, the conflicts, the legal rights, the shared home, the duties toward each other — can be described as marital. It is simply the adjective form of "marriage."

The condition or status of being married

"Marital status" is the most common phrase you'll encounter. It simply asks: are you married, single, divorced, or widowed? On official forms and documents, this is the standard term used to ask for that information.

Problems, conflict, or breakdown in a marriage

"Marital problems," "marital discord," and "marital breakdown" all describe trouble within a marriage. If a couple argues constantly, drifts apart, or their relationship deteriorates to the point of no return, these are marital problems. "Marital breakdown" specifically refers to the failure or collapse of a marriage.

Example: "They sought help before their marital problems became too serious to fix."

Happiness and harmony

On the positive side, "marital bliss" and "marital harmony" describe a happy, peaceful married life. "Marital satisfaction" is a term used especially in psychology to describe how fulfilled a person feels in their marriage.

Example: "The couple seemed to radiate marital bliss wherever they went."

Professional help for a struggling marriage

"Marital counseling" or "marital therapy" refers to sessions with a trained therapist that a couple attends to work through their difficulties. The aim is to repair and improve the relationship.

Legal and financial matters

"Marital assets" are things — property, money, investments — that belong to both spouses jointly as a result of their marriage. A "marital home" is the house a married couple shares. These terms come up frequently in legal contexts, especially during divorces.

Example: "During the divorce, the court divided the marital assets equally."

Rights, duties, and faithfulness

"Marital rights" and "marital duties" refer to the obligations and entitlements spouses have toward each other. "Marital fidelity" means being faithful and loyal to your spouse — not cheating on them.

Abuse and harm within a marriage

"Marital rape" and "marital abuse" are serious legal and social terms referring to assault or harm inflicted on a spouse within the marriage. These terms signal that marriage does not exempt anyone from accountability for harm.

"Marital" sits in the formal-to-neutral range. You'll find it most often in:

  • Legal language: marital assets, marital home, marital settlement
  • Psychology and medicine: marital therapy, marital satisfaction, marital conflict
  • Journalism and formal writing: marital breakdown, marital problems
  • Official forms and bureaucracy: marital status

In casual conversation, people more naturally say "my marriage is going through a rough patch" rather than "I'm having marital difficulties" — but in any written, professional, or official context, "marital" is perfectly natural and appropriate. It does not sound stiff or out of place there.

Several adjectives relate to marriage, but each carries a slightly different shade of meaning.

Matrimonial means essentially the same as marital — both mean "of or relating to marriage." However, matrimonial sounds more formal and legalistic. You'll more often see "matrimonial court" or "matrimonial law" in legal writing. In most everyday formal contexts, marital and matrimonial are interchangeable, but marital is far more commonly used.

Conjugal also relates to marriage, but it points specifically to the intimate, physical, or deeply personal side of the relationship between spouses. "Conjugal rights" historically referred to the right to physical intimacy in a marriage. A "conjugal visit" (in the context of prisons) is a private visit a prisoner is permitted with their spouse. Conjugal has a more private, intimate feel than marital, which is broader and more neutral.

Nuptial relates to the wedding ceremony and the act of getting married — not to the ongoing life of being married. "Nuptial vows," "nuptial ceremony," and "nuptial celebrations" all connect to the wedding event itself. You would not call a couple's long-running disagreements "nuptial problems" — that's where "marital" is the right word.

Spousal means "of or relating to a spouse" (the individual person you're married to). It is closely related to marital but focuses on the spouse as a person, rather than on the institution of marriage itself. "Spousal support" means financial support given to a spouse, particularly after separation or divorce. "Marital support" would gesture more broadly at the marriage relationship as a whole.

In short: marital is the most general and commonly used of these words. The others are either more formal, more specific, or more context-bound.

These two words are one of the most common sources of confusion in English because they look nearly identical:

  • Marital → relating to marriage
  • Martial → relating to war, soldiers, or military matters (as in "martial law," "martial arts," "court-martial")

The only spelling difference is the position of the letter "i." Always check which one you intend to write. Mixing them up produces absurd results — "martial bliss" and "marital arts" are both nonsensical.

Marital = relating to marriage or the relationship between spouses.

It is the go-to adjective for describing anything — a status, a conflict, a feeling, a legal matter, a right, a duty — that belongs to or flows from the institution of marriage. It is used across legal, psychological, journalistic, and official contexts. Among similar words (matrimonial, conjugal, nuptial, spousal), marital is the most general, most frequently used, and most versatile. And it must never be confused with martial, which belongs to the world of war and not of weddings.
